An abstract polymer model consists of a countable set $\Gamma$, a reflexive symmetric relation $\sim$ on $\Gamma$, and an activity function $z:\Gamma\to\mathbb C$. Its elements are called polymers, and $\gamma\sim\eta$ means that the two polymers are incompatible. A subset $X\subseteq\Gamma$ is compatible when no two distinct elements of $X$ are related by $\sim$. For each finite $V\subseteq\Gamma$, define the finite-volume partition polynomial

$$Z_V(z):=\sum_{\substack{X\subseteq V\\X\text{ compatible}}}\ \prod_{\gamma\in X}z_\gamma,$$

where the empty subset contributes $1$.

For $n\geq1$ and an ordered tuple $(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n)\in\Gamma^n$, let $\mathcal C_n$ be the finite set of connected simple graphs with vertex set $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, put $f_{ij}:=-\mathbf 1_{\{\gamma_i\sim\gamma_j\}}$, and define the connected coefficient

$$U_n(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n):=\sum_{G\in\mathcal C_n}\ \prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(G)}f_{ij}.$$

For $n=1$, $\mathcal C_1$ contains the one-vertex graph and the empty edge product equals $1$. These are finite polynomial and coefficient definitions; they assert no convergence.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim: Fix $n\geq2$ and a tuple $(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n)$, and let $H$ be its finite incompatibility graph: $\{i,j\}\in E(H)$ exactly when $\gamma_i\sim\gamma_j$. By [F1], $U_n=\sum_{G\subseteq H,\ G\text{ connected}}(-1)^{|E(G)|}$. Order the edges of the complete graph on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ lexicographically and assign their distinct ranks. Every connected subgraph $G$ has a spanning tree, and its finite set of spanning trees has one minimizing the sum of edge ranks. This minimum is unique: if distinct minimizing trees $T,S$ existed, take the least-ranked edge $e$ in their symmetric difference and, after swapping their names if needed, take $e\in T\setminus S$. Deleting $e$ from $T$ gives a cut crossed by the $S$-path between the endpoints of $e$; a crossing edge $f$ on that path lies in $S\setminus T$, and replacing $f$ by the earlier edge $e$ lowers the rank sum of $S$, a contradiction. For a tree $T$, let $A(T)$ contain the non-tree edges later than every edge on their unique $T$-path. If $G$ contains $T$ and a non-tree edge $e$ is earlier than a path edge $f$, then $T-f+e$ is a spanning tree of lower rank sum, so $T$ is not minimum. Conversely, if every non-tree edge of $G$ is later than every edge on its $T$-path, then for each $f\in T$ every other edge of $G$ crossing the cut made by deleting $f$ is later than $f$. If a competing spanning tree $S$ omitted $f$, the $S$-path between the endpoints of $f$ crosses this cut at an edge $e$; adding $f$ to $S$ and deleting that path edge $e$ gives a spanning tree with lower rank sum. Thus $T$ is the unique minimum tree of $G$ exactly when $T\subseteq G\subseteq T\cup A(T)$. Consequently, connected subgraphs of $H$ split into disjoint classes indexed by trees $T\subseteq H$, each class consisting of $T\cup A$ for $A\subseteq A(T)\cap E(H)$. The signed sum in one class is $(-1)^{n-1}(1-1)^{|A(T)\cap E(H)|}$, whose absolute value is at most $1$. Summing over those trees gives $|U_n(\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_n)|\leq\sum_{T\in\mathcal T_n}\prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(T)}\mathbf 1_{\{\gamma_i\sim\gamma_j\}}$. For $n=1$ both sides equal $1$.

For a fixed root label $1$ of type $\gamma$, let $S_\gamma^{(k)}$ be the nonnegative sum over all finite rooted labelled trees of height at most $k$, with root type fixed to $\gamma$, all other vertex types summed over $\Gamma$, each non-root vertex of type $\eta$ weighted by $|z_\eta|$, each edge weighted by $\mathbf 1_{\{\eta\sim\eta'\}}$, and each size-$n$ sum divided by $(n-1)!$. The root has weight $1$, so $S_\gamma^{(0)}=1$. At height at most $k+1$, the root has $m$ child subtrees of height at most $k$. For ordered subtree sizes $n_1,\ldots,n_m$, assigning the $n-1$ labels to the ordered branch vertex sets contributes $(n-1)!/(n_1!\cdots n_m!)$. In each branch there are $n_j$ choices for its child-root label; with the fixed-root subtree sum normalized by $(n_j-1)!$, the factor $n_j(n_j-1)!/n_j!$ is $1$. The parent normalization $(n-1)!$ therefore leaves the product of the branch weights, and division by $m!$ removes the ordering of the branches. Therefore, as an identity of nonnegative countable sums, $S_\gamma^{(k+1)}=\sum_{m=0}^\infty\frac1{m!}(\sum_{\eta\sim\gamma}|z_\eta|S_\eta^{(k)})^m=\exp(\sum_{\eta\sim\gamma}|z_\eta|S_\eta^{(k)})$. Countable sums here are suprema of finite subsums, so the identity follows first for finite type and size cutoffs and then by increasing limits. By [F2], $S_\gamma^{(0)}=1\leq e^{a_\gamma}$. If $S_\eta^{(k)}\leq e^{a_\eta}$ for every $\eta$, the assumed majorant [A1] gives $0\leq\sum_{\eta\sim\gamma}|z_\eta|S_\eta^{(k)}\leq a_\gamma$; [F3] then gives $S_\gamma^{(k+1)}\leq e^{a_\gamma}$. The nonnegative sums increase with $k$ and every finite tree has finite height, so their limit is the full rooted tree sum and is at most $e^{a_\gamma}$.

Apply the pointwise graph-to-tree bound of step 1.1 to each tuple in the definition of $R_\gamma$. All weights are nonnegative after taking absolute values, so summing over the countable polymer labels and then over $n$ preserves the inequality; the right side is the rooted tree sum bounded in step 1.2. Hence $R_\gamma\leq e^{a_\gamma}$.

Let $(\Gamma,\sim,z)$ be an abstract polymer model. Suppose $a:\Gamma\to[0,\infty)$ satisfies

$$\sum_{\eta\sim\gamma}|z_\eta|e^{a_\eta}\leq a_\gamma\qquad(\gamma\in\Gamma).$$

For each fixed root $\gamma\in\Gamma$, the nonnegative rooted connected-cluster sum

$$R_\gamma:=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac1{(n-1)!}\sum_{\gamma_2,\ldots,\gamma_n\in\Gamma}|U_n(\gamma,\gamma_2,\ldots,\gamma_n)|\prod_{j=2}^n|z_{\gamma_j}|$$

is well-defined as a possibly extended nonnegative series and satisfies $R_\gamma\leq e^{a_\gamma}$.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

Let $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_n(z-a)^n$ have radius $R$. If $|z-a|<R$, then $f$ is complex differentiable at $z$ and
$$f'(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}n c_n(z-a)^{n-1}.$$
Consequently $f$ is holomorphic on its open disc of convergence ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]).

derivations.claim: Write $f_{ij}=-\mathbf 1_{\{\gamma_i\sim\gamma_j\}}$. Reflexivity makes $\prod_{i<j}(1+f_{ij})$ zero when a tuple repeats a polymer, and otherwise this product is one exactly for a compatible subset. Hence $Z_V(t)=\sum_{n\geq0}\frac{t^n}{n!}\sum_{\vec\gamma\in V^n}(\prod_iw_{\gamma_i})\prod_{i<j}(1+f_{ij})$ as a formal series. Expanding the pair product gives all simple graphs. Each graph decomposes uniquely into a set partition of its vertex labels into connected components, and its weight factors over the blocks. The coefficient of $t^n$ in $\exp(L_V(t))$ is $\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_n}\sum_{\vec\gamma\in V^n}(\prod_{B\in\pi}U_{|B|}(\vec\gamma_B))(\prod_{i=1}^nw_{\gamma_i})$: the exponential's $1/k!$ removes ordering of the $k$ blocks, while assigning their labels contributes the multinomial factor that cancels the block factorials. This is exactly the connected-component decomposition of the all-graph coefficient, so $Z_V$ and $\exp(L_V)$ have identical formal coefficients.

Let $d_n$ be the coefficient of $t^n$ in $L_V$, and apply [F2] to the finite polymer set $V$ with activities $r w_\eta$. Condition [A1] implies its rooted criterion. For each fixed root $\gamma_1$, the $n$th nonnegative term of that rooted sum is at most $e^{a_{\gamma_1}}$; summing over roots and dividing by $n!$ gives $r^n|d_n|\leq\frac1n\sum_{\gamma\in V}r|w_\gamma|e^{a_\gamma}$. Thus on $|t|\leq s<r$, the series is dominated by a constant times $\sum_{n\geq1}(s/r)^n/n$, and its derivative series by a constant times $\sum_{n\geq1}(s/r)^{n-1}$. Both converge uniformly on every such closed subdisc.

By [F4], $L_V$ differentiates term by term throughout $|t|<r$. For each fixed $t$ with $|t|<r$, step 1.2 gives $\sum_{n\geq1}|d_n||t|^n<\infty$, so the total absolute sum after expanding $\exp(L_V(t))$ is at most $\sum_{k\geq0}(\sum_{n\geq1}|d_n||t|^n)^k/k!<\infty$. The products may therefore be regrouped by total degree; their coefficients are the formal coefficients identified in step 1.1, so $Z_V(t)=\exp(L_V(t))$ on the disc. By [F3], $\exp(L_V(t))\exp(-L_V(t))=1$, so $Z_V(t)$ is nonzero and $L_V$ is its analytic logarithm with $L_V(0)=0$.

Fix $d\geq1$. A pair potential is an even Borel function $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. For a finite list of positions $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, set $U_0=U_1=0$ and
$$U_N(X)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(x_i-x_j).$$
The value $+\infty$ is allowed and represents a forbidden configuration; $-\infty$ is not allowed.

The potential is **stable** if some finite $B\geq0$ satisfies $U_N(X)\geq-BN$ for every $N$ and every $X$. Fix a cell side $\ell>0$ and the half-open cubic tiling $C_k=\ell(k+[0,1)^d)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, and let $n_k(X)$ count the positions of $X$ in $C_k$. The potential is **cell-superstable** if there are constants $A_*>0$ and $B_*\geq0$ such that
$$U_N(X)\geq A_*\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}n_k(X)^2-B_*N$$
for every finite configuration; the sum is finite for finite $X$.

For disjoint finite cell-index sets $I,J$, let $W_{I,J}(X)$ be the sum of pair terms with one point in a cell indexed by $I$ and the other in a cell indexed by $J$. The potential is **lower regular** for this tiling if a nonnegative envelope $\Psi:\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{0\}\to[0,\infty)$ exists with $\sum_{k\ne0}\Psi(k)<\infty$ and
$$W_{I,J}(X)\geq-\sum_{k\in I}\sum_{l\in J}\Psi(k-l)n_k(X)n_l(X)$$
for all such $I,J,X$. The ordered-pair convention in this formula is fixed as written.

A **decreasing-integrable tail bound** means that for some $R_0\geq0$ there is a nonnegative nonincreasing function $\psi:[R_0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $|\phi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R_0$ and $\int_{R_0}^{\infty}\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty$. This explicit envelope condition is stronger than bare Lebesgue integrability of an arbitrary signed tail. Stability, cell-superstability, lower regularity, and a tail bound are separate properties; none is inferred from finite range alone.

$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of Borel measurable and Lebesgue measurable functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from A total pointwise product for extended-real-valued functions, and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
The positive and negative parts of a function. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space (Measure spaces). Equip
$\overline{\mathbb R}$ (The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined) with its order topology and let
$\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ be the corresponding Borel sigma-algebra
(The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space).

A function $f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ is **measurable** when
$f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Equivalently, it is enough to require
$$\{x\in X:f(x)>a\}\in\mathcal A \qquad \text{for every } a\in\mathbb R,$$
because the rays $(a,+\infty]$ generate $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

The **extended real line** is

$$\overline{\mathbb{R}} := \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty,+\infty\}$$

with the total order extending the usual order on $\mathbb{R}$ and satisfying
$-\infty < x < +\infty$ for every real $x$
([[def-extended-reals]]).

Its **Borel sigma-algebra** is the Borel sigma-algebra of that ordered
topological line in the sense of [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]. On this page it is
denoted $\mathcal{B}(\overline{\mathbb{R}})$ and is generated by the rays

$$\{\, (a,+\infty] : a \in \mathbb{R} \,\}.$$

In particular, $\{+\infty\}$ and $\{-\infty\}$ are Borel sets.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space) is Lebesgue
measurable (Lebesgue measurable sets, the family $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, and the restricted set function $\lambda_n$). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (Translation of a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Fix $n\geq2$ and positions $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, and put $f_{ij}=f_\beta(x_i-x_j)$. For each nonempty label set $I$, let $U_I=\sum_{i<j,\ i,j\in I}v(x_i-x_j)$. If $U_I=+\infty$, the adopted convention gives $e^{-2\beta U_I}=0$; otherwise all pair values in the sum are finite. In either case the exponential definition and addition law [F2], together with evenness of $v$, give $\prod_{i\in I}\prod_{j\in I\setminus\{i\}}|1+f_{ij}|=e^{-2\beta U_I}$. Stability and monotonicity [F1, F2] imply this product is at most $e^{2\beta B|I|}$. Writing $q_i=\prod_{j\in I\setminus\{i\}}|1+f_{ij}|$, all $q_i$ are nonnegative and their product is at most $e^{2\beta B|I|}$; hence some $r\in I$ has $q_r\leq e^{2\beta B}$.

The maps $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\mapsto x_i-x_j$ are continuous and hence Borel under [A1, F4]. Since $v$ is Borel [F1], composition with $v$ is Borel [F4]. The adopted map $u\mapsto e^{-\beta u}$ on $\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ is Borel: on $\mathbb R$ it is continuous by [F2], and its value at the Borel singleton $+\infty$ is $0$ by [F4]. Thus $f_\beta$ is Borel, and $U_n$ is a finite sum of finite products of Borel factors [F4]. The same composition and arithmetic facts on $\mathbb R^{dn}$ make each tree weight Borel. Repeated application of the two-factor identity in [F5] identifies the finite product Borel sigma-algebra, and the Borel-to-Lebesgue clause in [F5] makes the tree weight measurable for product Lebesgue measure.

For disjoint label sets $I,J$, define $g(I,J)$ as the sum of $\prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(G)}f_{ij}$ over simple graphs on $I\cup J$ in which every connected component meets $I$; set $g(\varnothing,\varnothing)=1$ and $g(\varnothing,J)=0$ for nonempty $J$. Evenness in [F1] makes each unordered-edge weight independent of which endpoint is written first. Choose $r\in I$ as in step 1.1 and put $I'=I\setminus\{r\}$. In each graph let $K\subseteq J$ be the neighbors of $r$ in $J$. Edges from $r$ to $I'$ are independently present or absent, and summing their two weights gives $\prod_{j\in I'}(1+f_{rj})$. Deleting $r$ leaves a graph all of whose components meet $I'\cup K$, and conversely any such graph reconstructs exactly one original graph after adjoining the chosen $r$-edges. Thus $g(I,J)=\left(\prod_{j\in I'}(1+f_{rj})\right)\sum_{K\subseteq J}\left(\prod_{k\in K}f_{rk}\right)g(I'\cup K,J\setminus K)$.

Under Countable Choice [A1], the product Lebesgue spaces are sigma-finite by [F3], so Tonelli [F6] applies. Root a labelled tree $T$ at $1$. A finite tree with at least two vertices has a leaf other than its root; integrate that leaf coordinate first. Translation invariance [F7] and evenness of $f_\beta$ give $\int_{\mathbb R^d}|f_\beta(x_\ell-x_j)|\,dx_\ell=C_\beta$. Repeating after each leaf deletion proves that the pinned tree integral is $C_\beta^{n-1}$.

Let $\mathcal F_I(J)$ be the forests on $I\cup J$ with exactly one vertex from $I$ in each tree, and define $h(I,J)=e^{2\beta B(|I|+|J|)}\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_I(J)}\prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(F)}|f_{ij}|$, with the same empty-root convention as $g$. For nonempty $I$, delete the root $r$ selected in step 1.1. Its component cannot contain another vertex of $I$, and the set $K\subseteq J$ of its neighbors gives exactly the roots of the resulting branches; this is a bijection with forests in $\mathcal F_{I'\cup K}(J\setminus K)$. The exponential addition law [F2] factors the size weight, so $h(I,J)=e^{2\beta B}\sum_{K\subseteq J}(\prod_{k\in K}|f_{rk}|)h(I'\cup K,J\setminus K)$. If $I=\varnothing$, both $g$ and $h$ are $1$ for $J=\varnothing$ and $0$ otherwise. Induct on $|I|+|J|$ from these base cases. Step 1.1 supplies the root bound and step 2.1 supplies the graph recurrence, giving $|g(I,J)|\leq q_r\sum_K(\prod_{k\in K}|f_{rk}|)|g(I'\cup K,J\setminus K)|$; the induction hypothesis and $q_r\leq e^{2\beta B}$ bound this by $h(I,J)$. At $I=\{1\}$, $J=\{2,\ldots,n\}$, $g(I,J)=U_n$ and every forest in $\mathcal F_I(J)$ is a spanning tree. This proves the pointwise tree bound.

In the Prüfer encoding, repeatedly delete the least-labelled leaf and record its neighbor; after $n-2$ deletions this gives a word of length $n-2$ over $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. At each stage a vertex occurs in the remaining word exactly once for each incident edge deleted before that vertex; it is recorded when a neighboring leaf is removed, and the vertex itself is deleted once it becomes a leaf, except for the final two vertices. Thus its occurrence count is its current degree minus one, and absence from the word is equivalent to being a current leaf. Conversely, from any such word, repeatedly join the least label absent from the remaining word to its first symbol and delete that label and symbol, then join the last two labels. Induction on the word length shows this constructs a tree: the absent label is a new leaf and the first symbol belongs to the remaining labels; after deleting that pair, the shorter word constructs the remaining tree. In the resulting tree the least absent label is a leaf and the first symbol is its neighbor, so encoding reverses every decoding step. The procedures give a bijection with all $n^{n-2}$ words. Integrating the pointwise tree bound of step 3.1 and using monotonicity, homogeneity and finite additivity [F8, F9] with the tree integral from step 2.2 yields $\int|U_n(0,x_2,\ldots,x_n)|\,dx_2\cdots dx_n\leq e^{2\beta Bn}n^{n-2}C_\beta^{n-1}$.

Fix $d\geq1$. A pair potential is an even Borel function $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. For a finite list of positions $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, set $U_0=U_1=0$ and
$$U_N(X)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(x_i-x_j).$$
The value $+\infty$ is allowed and represents a forbidden configuration; $-\infty$ is not allowed.

The potential is **stable** if some finite $B\geq0$ satisfies $U_N(X)\geq-BN$ for every $N$ and every $X$. Fix a cell side $\ell>0$ and the half-open cubic tiling $C_k=\ell(k+[0,1)^d)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, and let $n_k(X)$ count the positions of $X$ in $C_k$. The potential is **cell-superstable** if there are constants $A_*>0$ and $B_*\geq0$ such that
$$U_N(X)\geq A_*\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}n_k(X)^2-B_*N$$
for every finite configuration; the sum is finite for finite $X$.

For disjoint finite cell-index sets $I,J$, let $W_{I,J}(X)$ be the sum of pair terms with one point in a cell indexed by $I$ and the other in a cell indexed by $J$. The potential is **lower regular** for this tiling if a nonnegative envelope $\Psi:\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{0\}\to[0,\infty)$ exists with $\sum_{k\ne0}\Psi(k)<\infty$ and
$$W_{I,J}(X)\geq-\sum_{k\in I}\sum_{l\in J}\Psi(k-l)n_k(X)n_l(X)$$
for all such $I,J,X$. The ordered-pair convention in this formula is fixed as written.

A **decreasing-integrable tail bound** means that for some $R_0\geq0$ there is a nonnegative nonincreasing function $\psi:[R_0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $|\phi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R_0$ and $\int_{R_0}^{\infty}\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty$. This explicit envelope condition is stronger than bare Lebesgue integrability of an arbitrary signed tail. Stability, cell-superstability, lower regularity, and a tail bound are separate properties; none is inferred from finite range alone.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. All displayed integrals use Lebesgue measure. Let $d\geq1$, let $v:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ be an even Borel pair potential with no $-\infty$ values, and suppose it is stable with constant $B\geq0$. Fix $\beta>0$, set $e^{-c(+\infty)}:=0$ for every $c>0$, define the Mayer function $f_\beta(x):=e^{-\beta v(x)}-1$, and suppose

$$C_\beta:=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|f_\beta(x)|\,dx<\infty.$$

For $n\geq2$, let $\mathcal C_n$ be the connected simple graphs on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and put

$$U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n):=\sum_{G\in\mathcal C_n}\ \prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(G)}f_\beta(x_i-x_j).$$

For every configuration $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in(\mathbb R^d)^n$,

$$|U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)|\leq e^{2\beta Bn}\sum_{T\in\mathcal T_n}\ \prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(T)}|f_\beta(x_i-x_j)|,$$

where $\mathcal T_n$ is the set of labelled trees on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. In particular,

$$\int_{(\mathbb R^d)^{n-1}}|U_n(0,x_2,\ldots,x_n)|\,dx_2\cdots dx_n\leq e^{2\beta Bn}n^{n-2}C_\beta^{\,n-1}.$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $(X,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f_n:X\to\mathbb C$ be measurable with $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere. Suppose $g\ge0$ is measurable and $\int g\,d\mu<\infty$, and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for every $n$. Let $f_0(x)$ be the finite complex pointwise limit of $(f_n(x))$ where it exists, and $0$ elsewhere. Then $f_0$ is measurable, equals $f$ almost everywhere, is integrable, and $\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f_0\,d\mu$ and $\int|f_n-f_0|\,d\mu\to0$. If the specified $f$ is measurable, these same conclusions hold with $f$ in place of $f_0$. In particular this is automatic when $\mu$ is complete. On a noncomplete measure space an arbitrary almost-everywhere representative need not be measurable, so no integral of such a nonmeasurable $f$ is asserted.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (Translation of a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

Form the polynomial ring $\mathbb R[x]$
([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and define the **complex
numbers** by the quotient ring
$$\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$$
([[def-quotient-ring]]). Write $a$ for the constant class $a+(x^2+1)$ and set
$$i:=x+(x^2+1).$$
Thus $i^2=-1$ in the quotient. The constant-class map
$\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ is the specified real map; its injectivity and the
field structure are proved in [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], after which
$\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ is a field extension in the sense of
[[def-field-extension-generated-subfields-and-simple-extension]].

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

Let $f(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_n(z-a)^n$ have radius $R$. If $|z-a|<R$, then $f$ is complex differentiable at $z$ and
$$f'(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}n c_n(z-a)^{n-1}.$$
Consequently $f$ is holomorphic on its open disc of convergence ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from A total pointwise product for extended-real-valued functions, and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
The positive and negative parts of a function. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of Borel measurable and Lebesgue measurable functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space (Measure spaces). Equip
$\overline{\mathbb R}$ (The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined) with its order topology and let
$\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ be the corresponding Borel sigma-algebra
(The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space).

A function $f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ is **measurable** when
$f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Equivalently, it is enough to require
$$\{x\in X:f(x)>a\}\in\mathcal A \qquad \text{for every } a\in\mathbb R,$$
because the rays $(a,+\infty]$ generate $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

The **extended real line** is

$$\overline{\mathbb{R}} := \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty,+\infty\}$$

with the total order extending the usual order on $\mathbb{R}$ and satisfying
$-\infty < x < +\infty$ for every real $x$
([[def-extended-reals]]).

Its **Borel sigma-algebra** is the Borel sigma-algebra of that ordered
topological line in the sense of [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]. On this page it is
denoted $\mathcal{B}(\overline{\mathbb{R}})$ and is generated by the rays

$$\{\, (a,+\infty] : a \in \mathbb{R} \,\}.$$

In particular, $\{+\infty\}$ and $\{-\infty\}$ are Borel sets.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space) is Lebesgue
measurable (Lebesgue measurable sets, the family $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, and the restricted set function $\lambda_n$). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

(Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and their volume). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of Half-open boxes in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and their volume, and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ (Assuming countable choice, $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra containing every elementary set and $\lambda_n$ is a complete measure extending elementary volume).

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: For every $N$-point configuration, the energy $E_N=\sum_{i<j}v(x_i-x_j)$ is an extended-real Borel function: coordinate differences are continuous and hence Borel [F13], composition with $v$ preserves Borel measurability [F11], and finite sums preserve it wherever defined. The map $u\mapsto e^{-\beta u}$ on the extended real line, assigned $0$ at $+\infty$ and $+\infty$ at $-\infty$, is Borel because it is continuous on $\mathbb R$ [F12] and the endpoints are Borel [F14]. Thus the Boltzmann integrand is Borel on $\mathbb R^{dN}$. For $N\geq2$, repeated application of the two-factor product identity [F15] identifies the finite product Borel sigma-algebra; the Borel-to-Lebesgue inclusion [F16] then makes the integrand product-measurable. For $N=0$ or $1$ the same measurability is immediate from the empty or one-factor product. The same extended exponential map and the Borel potential show that $f_\beta$ is Borel. Stability [F1] gives $E_N\geq-BN$, so the integrand is at most $e^{\beta BN}$, with a forbidden $+\infty$ configuration contributing $0$. Since $|\Lambda_L|=(2L)^d<\infty$ [F17], the absolute value of the $N$th term of $\Xi_L(z)$ is at most $(|z|e^{\beta B}|\Lambda_L|)^N/N!$. The sum of these bounds is finite for every $z$ by [F7], so $\Xi_L$ is entire.

Stability at $N=2$ gives $v(x)\geq-2B$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$; hence $-1\leq f_\beta(x)\leq e^{2\beta B}-1$ by [F12]. Thus for each fixed $N$ every graph term in the finite expansion $\prod_{i<j}(1+f_\beta(x_i-x_j))$ is bounded and measurable on the finite-measure box $\Lambda_L^N$. Expanding the product gives a sum over all simple graphs; each graph decomposes uniquely into connected components. If the component sizes are $m_1,\ldots,m_k$, assigning the $N$ labels to an ordered list of blocks contributes $N!/\prod_jm_j!$, and division by $k!$ removes block order. Integrating a product over disjoint coordinate blocks factorizes by Fubini [F5], since the factors are bounded on finite-measure boxes. Therefore the coefficient of $z^N$ in $\Xi_L$ equals that in the formal exponential of $A_L(z):=\sum_{n\geq1}\frac{z^n}{n!}\int_{\Lambda_L^n}U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n$.

For $n\geq2$, integrate the pointwise tree estimate [F2] over $\Lambda_L^n$. Root each tree at vertex $1$, then remove leaves other than the root. At each removal the leaf integral over $\Lambda_L$ is at most the whole-space integral $C_\beta$ by monotonicity [F19] and translation invariance [F6]; Tonelli [F10] applies to the nonnegative tree products. The final root integral is $|\Lambda_L|$. The labelled-tree count in [F2] is $n^{n-2}$. Finite additivity [F20] sums those tree integrals, giving $\int_{\Lambda_L^n}|U_n|\leq e^{2\beta Bn}|\Lambda_L|n^{n-2}C_\beta^{n-1}$. Thus $U_n$ is integrable on $\Lambda_L^n$, and the integral triangle inequality [F18] gives $|b_n(L)|\leq e^{2\beta Bn}n^{n-2}C_\beta^{n-1}/n!$. The same bound holds for $|b_n|$ by the pinned estimate [F2].

Fix $n\geq2$ and write $y_1=0$, $y_i=x_i-x_1$ for $i\geq2$. Translation invariance of $U_n$ gives $U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=U_n(0,y_2,\ldots,y_n)$. By Tonelli [F10], translation invariance [F6], and the pinned integrability from [F2], $\int_{\Lambda_L^n}|U_n(x)|dx=\int_{(\mathbb R^d)^{n-1}}|U_n(0,y)|\,|\Lambda_L\cap(\Lambda_L-y_2)\cap\cdots\cap(\Lambda_L-y_n)|dy\leq|\Lambda_L|\int|U_n(0,y)|dy<\infty$, using the finite cube volume [F17]. Thus the integrand is absolutely integrable and Fubini [F5] applies. Translating each remaining coordinate in its section gives $b_n(L)=\frac1{n!}\int_{(\mathbb R^d)^{n-1}}U_n(0,y_2,\ldots,y_n)\theta_L(y)\,dy_2\cdots dy_n$, where $\theta_L(y)=\frac{|\Lambda_L\cap(\Lambda_L-y_2)\cap\cdots\cap(\Lambda_L-y_n)|}{|\Lambda_L|}=\prod_{j=1}^d(1-\frac{\max_i y_{i,j}-\min_i y_{i,j}}{2L})_+$, with $r_+=\max(r,0)$. For each fixed $y$, $0\leq\theta_L(y)\leq1$ and $\theta_L(y)\to1$. The cube-intersection volume formula follows from [F17]; $U_n$ is Borel by [F11, F13, F14, F15, F16], hence measurable. For every sequence $L_m\to\infty$, dominated convergence [F4] with majorant $|U_n(0,\cdot)|$ gives $b_n(L_m)\to b_n$. If the limit as a real variable $L\to\infty$ failed, some $\epsilon>0$ would have $|b_n(L)-b_n|\geq\epsilon$ for arbitrarily large $L$; Countable Choice [A1] selects such an $L_m\geq m$ for each $m$, contradicting the sequential conclusion. Hence $b_n(L)\to b_n$.

For every integer $n\geq2$, the positive series for $e^n$ in [F7] contains the term $n^n/n!$, so $n^{n-2}/n!\leq e^n/n^2$. If $C_\beta>0$, put $q(r)=rC_\beta e^{2\beta B+1}$. For $0<r$ with $q(r)<1$, step 1.3 yields $|b_n(L)|r^n\leq r e^{2\beta B+1}q(r)^{n-1}/n^2$ and $n|b_n(L)|r^{n-1}\leq e^{2\beta B+1}q(r)^{n-1}/n$; the same bounds hold for $b_n$. Both majorant series converge. If $C_\beta=0$, step 1.3 gives $b_n(L)=b_n=0$ for $n\geq2$. Thus the pressure series and their formal derivative series converge uniformly on every closed subdisc strictly inside $\mathcal D$; [F9] identifies the derivatives with the termwise derivatives.

The coefficient identity in step 1.2 is the formal identity $\Xi_L=\exp(A_L)$, and $A_L(z)=|\Lambda_L|p_L(z)$ by the definitions of $b_n(L)$. Fix a volume $L>0$ and a radius $r$ strictly inside $\mathcal D$. Step 2.1 gives $\sum_n|b_n(L)|r^n<\infty$, so $\sum_n|[z^n]A_L|r^n=|\Lambda_L|\sum_n|b_n(L)|r^n<\infty$ for this fixed volume. Expanding the complex exponential in [F8], the sum of absolute values of all terms is bounded by $\exp(\sum_n|[z^n]A_L|r^n)$; hence its products and coefficient sums may be regrouped, so the formal identity is an equality of convergent series and $\Xi_L(z)=\exp(|\Lambda_L|p_L(z))$. To pass to the limit on a compact subdisc $|z|\leq r$ inside $\mathcal D$, the pressure and derivative tails are uniformly bounded in $L$ by the convergent majorants of step 2.1. For each fixed $n$, step 1.4 gives coefficient convergence; finite partial sums and their derivatives therefore converge uniformly, and the uniform tail bounds give $p_L\to p$ and $p_L'\to p'$ uniformly there. [F8, F9, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.4, step 2.1] ∎

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix $d\geq1$. A pair potential is an even Borel function $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. For a finite list of positions $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, set $U_0=U_1=0$ and
$$U_N(X)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(x_i-x_j).$$
The value $+\infty$ is allowed and represents a forbidden configuration; $-\infty$ is not allowed.

The potential is **stable** if some finite $B\geq0$ satisfies $U_N(X)\geq-BN$ for every $N$ and every $X$. Fix a cell side $\ell>0$ and the half-open cubic tiling $C_k=\ell(k+[0,1)^d)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, and let $n_k(X)$ count the positions of $X$ in $C_k$. The potential is **cell-superstable** if there are constants $A_*>0$ and $B_*\geq0$ such that
$$U_N(X)\geq A_*\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}n_k(X)^2-B_*N$$
for every finite configuration; the sum is finite for finite $X$.

For disjoint finite cell-index sets $I,J$, let $W_{I,J}(X)$ be the sum of pair terms with one point in a cell indexed by $I$ and the other in a cell indexed by $J$. The potential is **lower regular** for this tiling if a nonnegative envelope $\Psi:\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{0\}\to[0,\infty)$ exists with $\sum_{k\ne0}\Psi(k)<\infty$ and
$$W_{I,J}(X)\geq-\sum_{k\in I}\sum_{l\in J}\Psi(k-l)n_k(X)n_l(X)$$
for all such $I,J,X$. The ordered-pair convention in this formula is fixed as written.

A **decreasing-integrable tail bound** means that for some $R_0\geq0$ there is a nonnegative nonincreasing function $\psi:[R_0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $|\phi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R_0$ and $\int_{R_0}^{\infty}\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty$. This explicit envelope condition is stronger than bare Lebesgue integrability of an arbitrary signed tail. Stability, cell-superstability, lower regularity, and a tail bound are separate properties; none is inferred from finite range alone.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. All displayed integrals use Lebesgue measure. Fix $d\geq1$, an even Borel pair potential $v:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ with no $-\infty$ values, stable with constant $B\geq0$, and $\beta>0$. Put $e^{-c(+\infty)}=0$ for every $c>0$, $f_\beta(x)=e^{-\beta v(x)}-1$, and $C_\beta=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|f_\beta(x)|\,dx<\infty$. For $n\geq2$, use

$$U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n):=\sum_{G\in\mathcal C_n}\prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(G)}f_\beta(x_i-x_j),$$

where $\mathcal C_n$ is the set of connected simple graphs on $\{1,\ldots,n\}$; set $U_1=1$. For $L>0$, let $\Lambda_L=[-L,L]^d$ and write $|\Lambda_L|:=\lambda_d(\Lambda_L)=(2L)^d$; define

$$\Xi_L(z):=\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^N}{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}\exp\!\left(-\beta\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}v(x_i-x_j)\right)\,dx_1\cdots dx_N,$$

with the $N=0$ term equal to $1$. Set $b_1(L)=1$ and, for $n\geq2$,

$$b_n(L):=\frac1{n!|\Lambda_L|}\int_{\Lambda_L^n}U_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\,dx_1\cdots dx_n.$$

Also set $b_1=1$ and, for $n\geq2$,

$$b_n:=\frac1{n!}\int_{(\mathbb R^d)^{n-1}}U_n(0,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\,dx_2\cdots dx_n.$$

Let $\mathcal D=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|e^{2\beta B+1}C_\beta<1\}$ when $C_\beta>0$, and let $\mathcal D=\mathbb C$ when $C_\beta=0$. On $\mathcal D$, the finite-volume connected pressure series $p_L(z):=\sum_{n\geq1}b_n(L)z^n$ and the limiting Mayer pressure series $p(z):=\sum_{n\geq1}b_nz^n$ converge absolutely and locally uniformly, are differentiable term by term, and satisfy

$$\Xi_L(z)=\exp\!\bigl(|\Lambda_L|p_L(z)\bigr),\qquad \lim_{L\to\infty}p_L(z)=p(z).$$

The convergence and derivative limits are uniform on every compact subdisc of $\mathcal D$. The pressure limit here is along centered cubes only.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $r>0$. Then the Euclidean ball $B(x,r)$ is
Lebesgue measurable and satisfies
$$0<\lambda(B(x,r))<\infty.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ (Order on the reals). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ (Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Ordered field):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric (Nonnegativity of a metric is a consequence of the other axioms, not an axiom) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear (Isometry, isometric embedding, and the subspace metric on a subset): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. A von Neumann natural is the set of its
predecessors, $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so it can be
used directly as an index set. Define

$$\mathbb{R}^n := \{\, x : x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\},$$

and write $x_k$ for $x(k)$, $k < n$. Two elements of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are equal
exactly when they agree at every $k < n$, functions being equal when they have
the same values. For $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ put

$$d_1(x,y) := \sum_{k<n} |x_k - y_k|, \qquad d_2(x,y) := \sqrt{\ \sum_{k<n} (x_k - y_k)^2\ }, \qquad d_\infty(x,y) := \max\{\, |x_k - y_k| : k < n \,\}.$$

All three are well defined: the finite sums are those of [[def-finite-sum]]; the
sum of squares is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[lem-of-square-positive]])
so it has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); and
$\{|x_k - y_k| : k < n\}$ is a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$, because
$n \ge 1$, so it has a maximum ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**Then $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$ are metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$**
([[def-metric-space]]).

**Why $n \ge 1$.** For $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^0$ has exactly one element,
the empty function, and $d_1$ and $d_2$ are the empty sum $0$ and its root; but
$d_\infty$ would be the maximum of the empty set, which does not exist. The
hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is therefore not decoration, and it is carried by every
statement about $d_\infty$ in this library.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), with open and closed sets
as in [[def-metric-topology]] and balls as in [[def-metric-ball]]. Then:

1. **Balls are open.** $B(x,r)$ is open, for every $x \in X$ and every $r > 0$.
2. **Arbitrary unions.** If $\mathcal{U}$ is any collection of open subsets of
   $X$, then $\bigcup \mathcal{U}$ is open.
3. **Finite intersections.** If $n \ge 1$ and $U_0, \dots, U_{n-1}$ are open,
   then $U_0 \cap \dots \cap U_{n-1}$ is open.
4. **Closed balls are closed.** $\bar B(x,r)$ is closed, for every $x \in X$ and
   every $r > 0$.

Together with the fact that $\emptyset$ and $X$ are open, recorded already in
[[def-metric-topology]], claims 2 and 3 say that $\mathcal{T}_d$ has exactly the
closure properties that the word *topology* names.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

The **extended real line** is

$$\overline{\mathbb{R}} := \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty,+\infty\}$$

with the total order extending the usual order on $\mathbb{R}$ and satisfying
$-\infty < x < +\infty$ for every real $x$
([[def-extended-reals]]).

Its **Borel sigma-algebra** is the Borel sigma-algebra of that ordered
topological line in the sense of [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]. On this page it is
denoted $\mathcal{B}(\overline{\mathbb{R}})$ and is generated by the rays

$$\{\, (a,+\infty] : a \in \mathbb{R} \,\}.$$

In particular, $\{+\infty\}$ and $\{-\infty\}$ are Borel sets.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),
On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
(Vector space over a field). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
(Nonnegative simple measurable functions) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure (Measures on sigma-algebras) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

derivations.claim: The Euclidean norm is even by [F5], so $v_a(-x)=v_a(x)$. The ball $B(0,a)$ is open, hence Borel, by [F4]; its complement is Borel as well. The target singleton $\{+\infty\}$ is Borel by [F4], and $\{0\}=\bigcap_{m\geq1}(-1/m,1/m)$ is Borel by the extended-real topology and sigma-algebra closure in [F4]. Since $v_a$ takes the constant value $+\infty$ on the ball and $0$ on its complement, the preimage of any target Borel set is among the empty set, the ball, its complement, and all of $\mathbb R^d$; hence $v_a$ is Borel. Every pair energy is either $0$ or $+\infty$, so every finite total energy is at least zero; therefore the stability inequality holds with $B=0$.

Under the stated convention, $e^{-\beta v_a(x)}-1=-1$ on $B(0,a)$ and $0$ elsewhere, so $|f_\beta|=\mathbf1_{B(0,a)}$. The ball lemma [F3] gives measurability and finite measure, and [F6] gives $C_\beta=\int\mathbf1_{B(0,a)}dx=|B(0,a)|\in(0,\infty)$.

The hypotheses of [F2] hold by steps 1.1–1.2 and [A1]. Substituting $B=0$ and $C_\beta=|B(0,a)|$ into its sufficient disk gives $e|z|\,|B(0,a)|<1$. This is a sufficient analytic domain; it is not asserted to be necessary and implies no freezing or coexistence point.
